_comment: Rate limits as DATA, not prose, so correcting one is a one-line pull request.
Every entry carries how we know it. The three values of `confidence` are not decoration:
MEASURED  - we saw it ourselves: a response header, or a 429 we walked into. `measured_on` says when.
DECLARED  - the provider says so on a page we read. `source` and `read_on` say where and when.
PAID-PLAN - the only published number belongs to a PAID tier, not the free one. Publishing it
as a free-tier figure is the mistake this repo calls out in its own README.
UNKNOWN   - nobody publishes it and we have not measured it. This stays UNKNOWN. We do not guess,
and we do not copy a number out of another list to fill the hole.
`scope` is the field most lists omit and it changes everything: a limit that applies per ORGANIZATION
or per PROJECT does not get bigger when you make another key.
`volatile: true` means this number moved under us at least once, or the provider stopped publishing it.
Re-measure before quoting it.
TWO KINDS OF FREE, AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME SHELF:
RECURRING  what you get every day, forever. This is what `all_models` and `models` describe.
ONE-TIME   a bundle handed over once at sign-up: a pot of tokens, or credits in money. Real
on day one, gone on day two. It lives in `one_time` and is NEVER added to the
daily figure - every list that adds them together is quoting a number that stops
being true after 24 hours.
A one-time grant in MONEY is not converted into tokens unless the provider publishes a price we
read ourselves. $5 of credits is $5 of credits until then.

groq.scope_quote: Rate limits apply at the organization level, not individual users.
groq.caveat: The published table is labelled as the BASE LIMITS OF THE DEVELOPER PLAN, not the free tier. Quote: 'the limits shown below are the base limits for the Developer plan'. Free-tier values are not published; check your own console at /settings/limits. Every list that reprints 1,000 requests/day as a free-tier figure is reprinting a paid plan's number.
groq.binding_limit: TPM, not RPD. 8,000 tokens per minute is what you actually hit: a long prompt returns 413 long before you approach 1,000 requests. We measured that 413 on an article-length prompt.

measured.note: Re-read from their headers on 2026-09-07 on the key: 1000 requests/day and 8000 tokens/minute. The per-minute token ceiling is what actually stops you - a long prompt returns 413 long before the request count matters.

cerebras.measured_how: rate-limit response headers on the calling account, read again on 2026-09-07: x-ratelimit-limit-requests-day 2400, x-ratelimit-limit-tokens-day 1000000, 5 requests/minute. The figures held across five days.
cerebras.caveat: Their pricing page on 2026-09-06 describes free access only as 'Free Trial: $5 in free credits after making an account' and publishes no daily free-tier ceiling at all. The numbers below are what the calling account's headers reported on 2026-09-02. They may be trial allowance rather than a standing free tier. Re-measure before relying on them.
cerebras.binding_limit: 5 requests per minute. Two calls inside the same minute need roughly 13 s between them.

one_time.quote: Free Trial: $5 in free credits after making an account
one_time.note: Their pricing page describes free access ONLY as this trial and publishes no daily free-tier ceiling. The 1,000,000 tokens/day above came from the calling account's headers and may be this trial rather than a standing tier.

google.source: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits and the AI Studio rate-limit console
google.caveat: The public docs page no longer prints the per-model table; it points you at aistudio.google.com/rate-limit, which needs a login. The figures below were read off that console screen. Free tier means literally 'no billing account linked': linking one moves the project to Tier 1 and off these numbers. Because the limits are per PROJECT, a second API key in the same project buys you nothing.

gemini-3.8-flash.note: The 20/day figure was read for 3.7 Flash on the same screen and is assumed to carry over to 3.8. Not separately confirmed. The 5/min WAS measured: our sixth call inside six seconds returned 429 with 'limit: 5'.

gemma-4-31b-it.note: Not published on the screen we read, and not measured.

google.binding_limit: Requests per DAY on the Flash models. 20/day is a handful of conversations, not a workload.

openrouter.caveat: The daily cap depends on lifetime credits purchased, and applies across ALL :free models combined, not per model. This condition is the one most lists drop, which makes their number wrong for a new account by a factor of twenty.

measured.note: 431 models listed on the public /models endpoint, of which 19 end in :free (4.4%)

cloudflare.caveat: The free allocation is denominated in NEURONS per day, not requests, and the neuron cost per token differs by more than a factor of ten between models: llama-3.2-1b costs 18,252 neurons per million output tokens, llama-3.3-70b costs 204,805. So a requests-per-day figure for 'Cloudflare' as a whole is meaningless. Convert per model or do not quote it.

nvidia.caveat: We carried a figure of 40 requests per minute per key in our own notes, but we could not find it on a public NVIDIA page when we went looking, so it is NOT published here as a rate limit. Unknown, not 40. What we do have is our own concurrency measurement below, which is worth more anyway: it says how many calls the model takes in parallel, which no rate-limit table tells you. If you find the published figure, the source URL is a one-line pull request.

measured_concurrency.moonshotai/kimi-k3: serial only: 7 of 8 concurrent calls returned 429 instantly. 25-55 s per call, so roughly 60-100 per hour if nothing else shares the key.

ollama.caveat: The free plan is $0 with 'starter usage credits included' and access to 'starter models' only, and the amount of those credits is not published. The API returns no rate-limit headers either, so the ceiling is genuinely unknown, not unlimited. Note also that 'run multiple models concurrently' is listed as a PAID plan feature and a higher tier advertises '10 concurrent requests', so the free plan should be assumed to be serial.
ollama.concurrency: assume 1 - concurrent execution is sold as a paid-plan feature

one_time.quote: Free accounts include a starter amount of usage for a smaller set of starter models. Adding extra credits unlocks all models.
one_time.note: They say a starter bundle exists and do not say how big it is. That is exactly what the row records: a grant we know about, with no number, because they publish none.

alibaba.caveat: Free access comes as per-model token grants with an expiry date rather than a standing rate limit, and the amount is not visible from the API. Reachable on the international endpoint. Unknown, not unlimited.

one_time.quote: Each model (such as qwen-plus, qwen3.6-plus, or qwen3.6-plus-2026-04-02) has its own independent free quota (typically 1,000,000 tokens). Quota cannot be merged or transferred across models.
one_time.expires_quote: The free quota is valid for 90 days, starting from the date you activate Alibaba Cloud Model Studio, the model is released, or your model request is approved (whichever is later).
one_time.note: 1,000,000 per model, and we track 4 of their models, so 4,000,000. The per-model split is THEIR rule, quoted above, not our multiplication: their own sentence says the quotas are independent and cannot be merged. Singapore region only, and calls stop when it is exhausted unless you complete account details, at which point you are billed.

xkiro.measured_how: their own usage endpoint, GET https://api.xkiro.com/v1/usage, which reports the daily token allowance and what is left of it
xkiro.caveat: The largest confirmed free token allowance in this list by a wide margin, and it took one GET to find - it was sitting behind an endpoint nobody had asked. Requests per day are NOT published; the ceiling here is tokens.
xkiro.binding_limit: Tokens, not requests. 5M/day is roughly 3,500 pages of output, so on this provider you will hit model quality or latency long before you hit the quota.

siliconflow.caveat: NOT TESTED, and this is about the caller, not about them: the key was answered with 402, so every call returned 402. That says nothing about the provider's free tier and SiliconFlow is therefore excluded from the quality ranking rather than scored zero.

one_time.quote: Flexible token pricing, high usage limits, and postpaid billing - plus $1 in free credits to get you started!
one_time.note: One dollar, in money, not tokens. We do not convert it: that needs their per-token price and a made-up conversion is a confident wrong number. On 2026-09-07 the endpoint answered HTTP 402 Payment Required, so the dollar is one-time and the endpoint stops serving after it.

uncloseai.caveat: No key, so there is no account to read a quota against, and the response carried no rate-limit headers at all. We measured that it answers; how much it will answer is genuinely unknown, and that is what the row says.
uncloseai.binding_limit: Unknown. The one thing measured is that a request with no credential returns a real completion.

ovhcloud.measured_how: Response headers on an anonymous POST: ratelimit-limit 2, x-ratelimit-limit-minute 2, the per-minute allowance header at 0, ratelimit-reset 44. Two attempts 90 seconds apart, both 429, both showing 0 left in the minute: the anonymous bucket is shared with every caller and was already empty both times.
ovhcloud.caveat: The per-minute ceiling is MEASURED. The daily figure is NOT, and multiplying 2 per minute by 1440 minutes would publish 2,880 requests a day that nobody can actually have: the bucket is shared with every anonymous caller on the internet and it was already empty both times we looked. rpd and tpd stay null on purpose.
ovhcloud.binding_limit: Requests per minute, at 2, shared with everyone. This is what a free tier with no sign-up actually costs: you are queueing behind the whole internet.

mistral.measured_how: Their own rate-limit headers, read seven times on 2026-09-07. The ceiling the calling account is given MOVES, and not slowly: at 00:05 UTC the headers said x-ratelimit-limit-tokens-minute 625000 and the call returned a completion. Five readings between 00:39 and 00:43 UTC, one minute apart, all said x-ratelimit-limit-req-minute 0 and every call was refused with 429. Earlier the same day, before that, the headers also said 0.
mistral.caveat: A limit of ZERO is not a limit reached, it is a tier that is not switched on. the calling account swung from 0 to 625,000 tokens a minute and back to 0 within an hour, so the large figure is NOT capacity you can plan on and it is not published here as one. Whatever conditions turn this tier on - phone verification, region, a queue - are not stated on any page we could find, and their tier documentation URL now returns 404.
mistral.binding_limit: Whether the tier is on at all. Six of our seven readings today were refused.

kenari.measured_how: response headers on a normal completion: a limit header of 5 with a reset timestamp. The unit is not stated in the header name.
kenari.caveat: 13 of their 72 models carry a :free suffix and those are the only ones listed here. The rest are pay-as-you-go, and a catalogue that reports zero cost for all 72 is reporting missing prices, not a giveaway.
kenari.binding_limit: Unknown. A limit of 5 with no unit could be per minute or per something else, and we will not guess which.

aihubmix.caveat: 54 of their 417 models carry a -free suffix; only those are listed. Their billing endpoint reports a hard limit of $100,000,000, which is a placeholder rather than a quota, so it is not recorded as one.
aihubmix.binding_limit: Unknown. Nothing they expose says how much of the free models you may use.

inferx.caveat: The endpoint answered with the key and returned a real completion. No rate-limit headers, no usage endpoint, nothing published we could find.

unorouter.caveat: 163 of their 262 models carry a :free suffix. The endpoint answered a real completion on 2026-09-07 and returned no rate-limit headers of any kind, so how much of it you may use is unknown. Image models on the same catalogue answer 'invalid api type' - the free text models are the ones listed here.
